hero.headline: CIA director questions Iran's commitment to nuclear concessions
hero.teaser: CIA Director John Ratcliffe told senior officials that US intelligence raises doubts about Iran's willingness to make nuclear concessions.
hero.body:
CIA Director John Ratcliffe has told President Trump and other senior officials that intelligence gathered by US agencies has raised serious doubts about Iran's willingness to make the nuclear concessions the US is seeking in any final deal, according to sources familiar with those discussions.

Ratcliffe is not alone in his skepticism within Trump's top team. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth have both expressed concerns and raised questions about the deal in internal discussions, according to two sources. The divided views among senior officials reflect broader uncertainty about Iran's intentions as the two countries prepare for 60 days of nuclear negotiations.

The skepticism comes as the administration moves forward with a memorandum of understanding signed digitally over the weekend. Senior US officials told reporters that the MOU is only the initial step toward a broader agreement. The agreement between the US and Iran is intended to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and kick-start the 60-day negotiation period, with the deal set to be signed in person on Friday.

In contrast to the concerns raised by Ratcliffe, Rubio, and Hegseth, Vice President Vance and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have advocated for the deal, according to sources familiar with the discussions.

The skepticism about Iran's nuclear intentions carries significant weight given recent diplomatic history. Previous nuclear negotiations have been complicated by misunderstandings about Iran's nuclear program, including disagreements over technical aspects and the scope of Iran's planned nuclear activities.

The ongoing negotiations represent an attempt to resolve a conflict that began on February 28 and disrupted energy production and transportation across the Middle East. Oil prices jumped when the fighting began, and the new agreement aims to stabilize global energy markets by reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

This is not the first time US officials have had to navigate nuclear discussions with Iran. The Obama administration previously conducted extensive nuclear negotiations, sending 10 senior officials from four different departments to talks in Vienna in 2009. Those negotiations stretched over three 24-hour days, with negotiators in constant touch with Washington to check details of the proposed deal.

The Trump administration's current negotiating team appears leaner. Sources indicate that the talks leading up to the current MOU involved limited technical expertise and support compared to previous diplomatic efforts.

The next 60 days will be crucial for determining whether the two countries can reach a comprehensive nuclear agreement. The internal divisions among US officials suggest that reaching consensus on Iran's nuclear program will require navigating significant disagreements about Iran's reliability as a negotiating partner and the likelihood of achieving US objectives.

cards.headline: U.S. and Iran Sign Preliminary Deal to End War, but Terms Remain Secret
cards.teaser: President Trump and Iran's lead negotiator have signed a preliminary agreement expected to end hostilities and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, but the administrati.
cards.body:
President Trump and Iran's lead negotiator have signed a preliminary agreement aimed at ending the conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway through which roughly a fifth of global oil supplies flows. Trump announced that the strait will reopen from Friday.

The administration has not released the agreement's specific terms. Congress members from both parties—including Republicans—said they lack information about the deal's contents. NPR reports the agreement represents a major breakthrough but leaves critical issues for further negotiations.

cards.headline: Eight dead after Air Force B-52 bomber crashes at California base
cards.body:
Eight people are presumed dead after a B-52 Stratofortress bomber crashed shortly after takeoff at Edwards Air Force Base in California's Mojave Desert on Monday morning, officials confirmed.

The aircraft went down at approximately 11:20 a.m. during what the base described as a routine test mission. "Initial indications are that the crash was not survivable," Edwards Air Force Base stated in a Monday afternoon announcement. Emergency response personnel responded to the scene, and officials worked to account for all personnel involved.

The Boeing B-52 Stratofortress has served as a cornerstone of the US military's long-range bomber fleet since the 1950s. The aircraft continues to play a critical role in the Air Force's operations, supporting missions ranging from conventional bombing to nuclear deterrence. The military operates dozens of these bombers across multiple bases nationwide.

Edwards Air Force Base functions as a major testing and research facility for the Air Force. The base has historically served as a proving ground for experimental aircraft and aerospace development programs. The crash marks a significant incident for the installation.

The Air Force has not released the identities of those killed or provided details about whether all casualties were crew members. Investigators are expected to examine the wreckage and flight data to determine what caused the accident. The agency has not disclosed additional information about the circumstances surrounding the crash.

The B-52 fleet has undergone numerous upgrades throughout its decades of service, and the Air Force has committed to keeping the aircraft operational for years to come. Despite its age, the platform remains essential to the military's strategic capabilities.

This crash adds to the scrutiny facing military aviation safety. Edwards Air Force Base will likely face intensive investigation as officials work to understand how the incident occurred and whether all safety protocols were properly followed.

The loss represents one of the deadliest incidents involving a B-52 in recent memory. As the investigation continues, the Air Force will work to determine whether the aircraft was experiencing any known technical issues prior to takeoff and what factors may have contributed to the crash shortly after departure.

cards.headline: UK Imposes Fresh Energy Sanctions on Russia at G7 Summit
cards.teaser: Britain announced new sanctions targeting Russian energy sector during the G7 meeting in France.
cards.body:
Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced additional sanctions against Russia during the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains, France, pledging to "choke off" Russian revenue streams. The measures target Russia's finance networks and shadow fleet vessels used to transport oil and gas while circumventing existing sanctions. Starmer committed to standing with Ukraine "for as long as it takes."

The UK is also providing hundreds of millions of pounds in energy support for Ukraine, including nuclear energy assistance. The sanctions represent Britain's continued effort to increase economic pressure on Moscow while bolstering Ukraine's energy infrastructure.

cards.headline: Ukraine Advances Bid to Join European Union
cards.teaser: Negotiations are beginning for Ukraine to join the EU, though the process is expected to take years.
cards.body:
Ukraine has begun formal negotiations to join the European Union after its biggest opponent within the bloc stopped blocking the process. This marks a significant milestone in Ukraine's westward integration efforts.

Full EU membership will require Ukraine to undertake extensive legal, economic, and institutional reforms. The country must align its laws and regulations with EU standards across multiple sectors. While negotiations have officially started, the complete accession process is expected to take years to complete.

cards.headline: Ukraine Uses AI to Counter Russian Drone Attacks
cards.teaser: Ukrainian forces are deploying autonomous technologies trained on wartime data to intercept Russian drones.
cards.body:
Ukraine has developed AI-powered interceptor systems to shoot down Russian drones targeting its infrastructure and military positions. These autonomous technologies are trained on extensive data collected throughout the war, enabling them to identify and engage hostile drones more effectively than conventional defense methods.

The adoption of AI-driven defenses demonstrates how modern warfare increasingly relies on technological innovation. By analyzing vast amounts of battlefield information, Ukraine's systems represent a significant shift toward data-driven military strategies in countering the persistent aerial threat posed by Russian operations.

cards.headline: UK Announces Social Media Ban for Children Under 16
cards.teaser: Prime Minister Keir Starmer said his government planned to bar children under 16 from social media platforms.
cards.body:
The British government announced plans to ban children under 16 from using social media platforms, following similar measures adopted in Australia and other countries. Prime Minister Keir Starmer outlined the proposal as part of efforts to protect young people from online harms.

Questions remain about how the ban would be enforced and which platforms would be covered. Social media companies have pushed back against the measure, though specific details of their objections have not been made public. The proposal would make the UK the latest country to impose age restrictions on social media access.

cards.headline: Protests Erupt in France After Killing of 11-Year-Old Girl
cards.teaser: Public anger has grown after authorities revealed a suspect in the death of Lyhanna Rameau Bernard had been previously flagged to law enforcement.
cards.body:
Demonstrations have spread across France following revelations that a man accused of kidnapping and killing 11-year-old Lyhanna Rameau Bernard had been previously reported to police. The girl's death earlier this month has sparked widespread outrage directed at the French justice system.

The protests reflect mounting public frustration over perceived failures by authorities to act on warning signs about dangerous individuals. The case has intensified scrutiny of how law enforcement handles reports about potential threats and whether existing procedures adequately protect the public. The demonstrations represent some of the most significant public anger directed at the justice system in recent months.

cards.headline: Greek Court Orders Convicted Militant Leader Back to Prison
cards.teaser: Alexandros Giotopoulos, serving 17 life sentences, has been ordered to return to custody.
cards.body:
An 82-year-old Alexandros Giotopoulos, who leads the leftist militant group November 17, has been ordered back to prison by a Greek court. Giotopoulos is serving 17 life sentences for his role in the organization.

November 17 carried out bombings and assassinations across Greece over several decades, targeting politicians, businesspeople, and foreign officials. The group's members were arrested in the early 2000s. The court revoked Giotopoulos's release status, returning him to full custody.

cards.headline: California governor says Justice Department investigating him and his wife
cards.teaser: Gavin Newsom said the Trump administration has opened an investigation into him and his wife.
cards.body:
California Governor Gavin Newsom said on Monday that the Justice Department is investigating him and his wife, Jennifer Siebel Newsom. In a video statement, he claimed that federal agents had recently contacted family friends and former employees, seeking records as part of the inquiry.

Newsom attributed the investigation to President Trump, saying the administration is "coming after me because I am considering running for president." He characterized the effort as an attempt to find a crime and accused authorities of abusing the grand jury process.

cards.headline: Kennedy Center removes Trump's name from building
cards.teaser: The Kennedy Center has taken down Trump's name from the exterior, though a tarp currently covers the area where it appeared.
cards.body:
The Kennedy Center removed President Trump's name from its building in Washington. A tarp now covers the exterior section where the name previously appeared, blocking the proof of removal from public view.

The tarp has remained in place for days following the removal. The Kennedy Center has not explained why the covering persists or when it will come down.

cards.headline: Vice President Vance writes about Vatican meeting in new book
cards.teaser: J.D. Vance describes a meeting at the Vatican last year as unsettling in a newly published book.
cards.body:
Vice President J.D. Vance published a new book that places his Catholic faith at the center of his personal story and political identity. The book describes a meeting at the Vatican last year that Vance found unsettling.

Vance also addressed past comments in the book, calling his childless cat ladies remark one of the dumbest things he ever said. The book explores his religious conversion and how it has shaped his worldview.

cards.headline: Former ICE director takes consulting role in national security
cards.teaser: Todd Lyons, who previously led Immigration and Customs Enforcement, has accepted a consulting position focused on national security and defense.
cards.body:
Todd Lyons, the former director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, has taken on a consulting role focused on national security and defense. However, federal law prevents him from working with the Department of Homeland Security for one year following his departure from the agency.

This one-year restriction is part of ethics regulations meant to prevent former government officials from immediately consulting or lobbying their previous employers. During this period, Lyons will direct his consulting efforts toward national security matters outside the DHS's purview.

cards.headline: Thames Water rescue deal faces government objection
cards.teaser: The British government objected to a proposed rescue deal for Thames Water, pushing the utility closer to potential nationalization.
cards.body:
Thames Water moved closer to nationalization after the British government objected to a proposed rescue deal for the struggling utility. A government spokesman told the BBC that the current offer does not do enough to protect consumers or the environment.

The objection increases the likelihood that the government will take control of Thames Water, which serves millions of customers in and around London. The utility has faced financial difficulties and criticism over infrastructure failures and pollution incidents.

cards.headline: Australian watchdog calls reality show allegations disturbing
cards.teaser: Australia's media regulator described allegations about Married at First Sight Australia as disturbing.
cards.body: Australia's communications regulator has described allegations involving Married at First Sight Australia as disturbing. The claims have drawn international attention, with the UK's media watchdog Ofcom also weighing in on the matter, calling the allegations deeply concerning. Both regulators have acknowledged the issue, signaling potential scrutiny of the popular reality television program.

hero.headline: Fox Acquires Roku for $22 Billion in Streaming Expansion
hero.body:
Fox has agreed to purchase streaming device maker Roku for $22 billion, marking one of the largest media acquisitions in recent years. The deal represents a significant strategic shift for Fox as it seeks to expand its presence in the streaming video market and gain direct access to millions of viewers who use Roku devices to watch content.

The acquisition gives Fox control over one of the most widely used streaming platforms in the United States. Roku operates both a line of streaming devices and a free, ad-supported streaming service, positioning Fox to compete more directly with tech giants and other media companies in the evolving digital landscape. The deal combines Fox's content library and live programming capabilities with Roku's distribution platform and viewer data.

For Fox, the purchase represents a bet on advertising-supported streaming as a growing revenue source. Unlike subscription-based services, Roku has built its business around free content funded by advertisements, a model that aligns with Fox's traditional broadcast television approach. Industry analysts note that owning both content and distribution infrastructure could give Fox more leverage in negotiating with other content providers and advertisers.

The transaction also reflects broader consolidation in the media and technology sectors as traditional broadcasters seek to adapt to changing viewer habits. Streaming has increasingly replaced cable and satellite television, prompting legacy media companies to pursue partnerships and acquisitions that offer direct connections to audiences. The deal is subject to regulatory approval, though the combined company would still face competition from established streaming services and other platforms.

Media buyers and advertising executives have expressed interest in how Fox plans to integrate Roku's advertising technology with its own sales operations. Roku has developed sophisticated targeting capabilities that allow advertisers to reach specific audiences, a feature that could enhance Fox's appeal to marketers seeking alternatives to traditional television buys.

cards.headline: Nvidia Plans to Raise $25 Billion Through Bond Sale
cards.teaser: The chipmaker is entering the debt market for the first time in five years as it seeks capital amid surging demand for AI processors.
cards.body:
Nvidia is launching its first corporate bond offering since 2021, seeking to raise over $25 billion. This debt sale marks the chipmaker's initial major borrowing since the artificial intelligence boom began.

The bond issuance comes as investors test their appetite for further exposure to the AI sector amid increased borrowing activity across the technology industry. The move allows Nvidia to access capital markets while maintaining its strong market position driven by demand for its AI-focused graphics processors.

cards.headline: SpaceX IPO Raised $87.5 Billion, Exceeding Initial Estimates
cards.teaser: The space company's public offering brought in $10 billion more than originally reported, marking one of the largest IPOs on record.
cards.body:
SpaceX's initial public offering brought in $87.5 billion, surpassing the previously reported $75 billion figure. The company's underwriters fully exercised their share purchase options, contributing to the larger final amount. This makes the offering one of the largest in stock market history.

The strong investor demand pushed SpaceX shares up more than 35 percent during its first two days of trading. The successful debut reflects broad market confidence in the space industry and SpaceX's leadership in satellite launches and spacecraft development.

cards.headline: Thames Water Moves Closer to Government Takeover After Rescue Deal Rejected
cards.teaser: UK officials objected to a proposed rescue plan for the troubled water utility, citing inadequate protections for consumers and the environment.
cards.body:
The British government has rejected a rescue deal for Thames Water, objecting that the current offer does not do enough to protect consumers or the environment. This decision moves the struggling utility company closer to potential nationalization.

Thames Water has faced significant challenges including infrastructure failures and financial instability. The government's rejection of the proposed rescue package indicates officials may pursue public ownership if private investors cannot present an acceptable alternative solution.

cards.headline: Justice Department Approves Paramount Acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery
cards.teaser: Federal regulators cleared the merger despite internal questions, while state attorneys general raise concerns beyond traditional antitrust issues.
cards.body:
Donald Trump's Department of Justice has approved the $111 billion merger of Paramount Skydance, controlled by the Ellison family, and Warner Bros. Discovery. The antitrust division completed its review after months of examination, despite concerns from entertainment and media industry figures about reduced competition.

The combined company will merge two major news networks—Paramount's CBS News and CNN—along with film studios, television networks, and streaming services. The deal still faces scrutiny from UK regulators and potential lawsuits from state attorneys general, who are examining issues beyond standard antitrust considerations.

cards.headline: Stock Markets Rise as Oil Prices Fall Following US-Iran Agreement
cards.teaser: Equities gained and energy costs dropped after the two countries reached a preliminary deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
cards.body:
US stock markets rose and oil prices fell following an announcement that the United States and Iran have agreed on a framework to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed more than 450 points to a record close, while the Nasdaq also opened higher. President Trump confirmed the deal would allow the key waterway to reopen.

Crude oil prices dropped as markets responded to the potential agreement. The Strait of Hormuz is a critical passage for global oil shipments, and reopening it could allow more energy and goods to flow through the waterway.

cards.headline: UK Plans Social Media Ban for Children Under 16
cards.teaser: Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced the government intends to prohibit minors from accessing social media platforms.
cards.body:
Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced the UK government will ban children under 16 from using social media platforms including Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, Facebook, and X. The policy would require social media companies to implement age verification systems, with the government aiming to enact the restrictions by next spring.

Major technology companies have pushed back against the proposal. Meta, YouTube, and Snapchat argue the ban will drive teenagers toward less safe platforms and services. The announcement reflects growing government concerns about social media's impact on young people's mental health and development.

hero.headline: Brain implant allows man with ALS to communicate independently at home
hero.body:
A man living with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has achieved independent communication using an implanted brain-computer interface over an extended period at home, according to research published in Nature. The study documents the long-term use of an intracortical device that enabled speech and cursor control without requiring constant supervision from medical professionals or researchers.

The participant successfully used the brain implant system independently in his daily environment, marking a shift from laboratory-controlled demonstrations to practical home application. The interface translated brain signals into text and cursor movements, allowing the user to communicate and control devices. The research team characterized the participant as the first power user of such a system, having generated approximately two million words over a two-year period through the device.

The technology works by recording neural activity directly from the brain's motor cortex, the region responsible for movement planning and execution. These signals are then decoded by algorithms that interpret the user's intended actions, whether forming words or moving a cursor on a screen. The system's accuracy and reliability in an unsupervised home setting represents a significant advance from earlier brain-computer interfaces that required laboratory conditions and technical support.

ALS progressively destroys motor neurons, the nerve cells that control voluntary muscle movement. As the disease advances, patients lose the ability to speak, move, and eventually breathe independently, while cognitive function typically remains intact. This creates what researchers describe as a locked-in state, where individuals cannot communicate despite full awareness. Current treatment options focus on symptom management rather than halting disease progression.

The successful home deployment of this brain-computer interface demonstrates the technology's potential to restore communication independence for people with severe motor disabilities. The two-year timeframe and high volume of generated text suggest the system remained functional and usable over extended periods without degradation. The research indicates that such devices could transition from experimental prototypes to practical assistive tools for patients with paralysis or severe motor impairment.

cards.headline: Chinese rocket breaks apart near Starlink satellites, creating space debris
cards.teaser: A Chinese rocket fragmented in orbit close to SpaceX's Starlink constellation, generating an estimated 100 to 150 new pieces of orbital debris.
cards.body:
A Chinese rocket broke apart in orbit in proximity to SpaceX's Starlink satellite network. The breakup occurred at an altitude where the constellation operates, raising concerns about collision risks.

The fragmentation likely produced between 100 and 150 new pieces of space junk. These fragments join the growing population of debris in low Earth orbit, where thousands of satellites and debris pieces already travel at high velocities.

cards.headline: NASA unveils space telescope 1,000 times faster than Hubble
cards.teaser: NASA introduced the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, designed to operate at speeds vastly exceeding the Hubble Space Telescope's capabilities.
cards.body:
NASA introduced the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, an observatory designed to survey the cosmos at speeds 1,000 times faster than the Hubble Space Telescope. The telescope features a mirror originally developed for spy satellites, enabling it to cover significantly larger areas of sky in shorter timeframes.

The Roman telescope represents a major advancement in how astronomers will map the universe. NASA has launched a program inviting the public to submit their names to be included aboard the telescope when it launches.

cards.headline: UK plans to ban social media for children under 16
cards.teaser: The British government announced plans to prohibit social media access for children under 16 and may introduce overnight usage restrictions.
cards.body:
The United Kingdom plans to ban social media for users under 16, with the government aiming to enact the restrictions by next spring. The ban would apply to major platforms including Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, Facebook, and X.

Major technology companies including Meta, YouTube, and Snapchat have criticized the proposal, arguing that it will drive teenagers toward less safe and more harmful platforms. The ban was announced by Prime Minister Keir Starmer.

cards.headline: Microsoft plans to close Hellblade developer Ninja Theory
cards.teaser: Xbox owner Microsoft is shutting down Ninja Theory, the game studio that created the Hellblade series, as part of broader restructuring.
cards.body:
Microsoft is shutting down Ninja Theory, the studio behind the Hellblade series. Staff members learned about the closure during a call on Monday. The company is hoping to find a buyer for the studio.

The shutdown is part of broader cuts affecting multiple Xbox studios under Microsoft, including Compulsion Games and Double Fine.

cards.headline: SpaceX completes first launch as publicly traded company
cards.teaser: SpaceX successfully launched a Falcon 9 rocket carrying Starlink satellites, marking its first mission since debuting on the Nasdaq stock exchange.
cards.body:
SpaceX completed its first Falcon 9 launch as a publicly traded company, deploying 24 Starlink satellites from Vandenberg Space Force Base. The mission marked a significant milestone following the company's Nasdaq debut.

The launch came after SpaceX's stock market listing valued the aerospace manufacturer at $2.2 trillion. The successful mission demonstrated operational continuity as SpaceX transitions into its new role as a public company.

cards.headline: Apple releases major Siri overhaul in iOS 27
cards.teaser: Apple deployed a significant update to its Siri voice assistant in iOS 27, representing the third generation of the company's foundation models.
cards.body:
Apple has unveiled a significantly redesigned Siri featuring third-generation foundation models as part of iOS 27. The update represents the company's effort to strengthen its position in artificial intelligence and addresses long-standing concerns about Siri's capabilities relative to competitors like Google and Amazon.

The release came as Tim Cook bid farewell in his role at the company. Apple also announced new child safety features alongside the Siri update, responding to ongoing concerns about harmful applications.

hero.headline: Cape Verde holds Spain to scoreless draw in World Cup debut
hero.body:
Cape Verde achieved a remarkable feat in their inaugural World Cup appearance, securing a 0-0 draw against Spain in Atlanta. The debutant nation's resilient defense and outstanding goalkeeping prevented one of the tournament's favored teams from scoring, marking a significant upset in World Cup opening matches.

The performance centered on 40-year-old goalkeeper Vozinha, who delivered a standout display with seven crucial saves. Named player of the match, Vozinha made his mark on World Cup history while facing an emotional moment off the pitch. Unable to afford a US visa, his mother missed the historic match. The goalkeeper later expressed that he had "worked my whole life for this moment" and wished he could have shared it with his late grandparents and his mother.

Spain dominated possession with 24 shots on goal but failed to break through Cape Verde's organized defensive structure. The European champions extended a concerning streak, reaching 2,500 passes since their last World Cup goal. Despite introducing teenager Lamine Yamal in the 70th minute, Spain could not find the breakthrough.

Cape Verde created genuine opportunities despite their underdog status. In the final minutes, Diney Borges headed wide in the 90th minute, while Ryan Mendes had another chance three minutes later. Pico Lopes, a former Shamrock Rovers player from Dublin, made a crucial block on 88 minutes to deny Dani Olmo. Lopes' journey to the World Cup itself tells a remarkable story. Initially contacted by Cape Verde's coaching staff via LinkedIn, he ignored the first message assuming it was spam because it was in Portuguese. A follow-up message in English nine months later eventually brought him to the squad.

Coach Bubista had emphasized that his team's qualification represented more than just football, encompassing music and culture. His tactical approach prioritized strong defensive organization while maintaining the courage to attack. The strategy proved effective, as Cape Verde matched Spain's intensity throughout the match.

The result carries significant meaning for a nation of 600,000 people making their World Cup debut. The starting eleven included players from eight different leagues, with most competing outside elite football. Their resistance against the European champions provided vindication of their place on the world stage and positioned them favorably in their group standings.

The draw generated unexpected consequences in the betting world, with one sports bettor reportedly losing $1 million wagering against Cape Verde. For the island nation's supporters, the result represented an arrival moment for their football program on the global stage. The historic draw will be remembered as a moment when a determined underdog challenged and held one of the world's best teams.

cards.headline: Belgium draws 1-1 with Egypt after own goal denies African side first World Cup win
cards.teaser: An own goal from Mohamed Hany gave Belgium a 1-1 draw with Egypt at the Seattle Stadium.
cards.body:
Egypt were on the verge of a historic first World Cup victory before an own goal from Mohamed Hany earned Belgium a 1-1 draw. The Pharaohs had taken the lead and held it through much of the match at Seattle Stadium.

Belgium manager Rudi Garcia turned to his bench in the second half, introducing record goalscorer Romelu Lukaku. The striker's presence immediately shifted the dynamic—his threat drew two defenders into the box on his first run, creating the opportunity for the own goal that salvaged a point for the European side.

cards.headline: Kentucky hires Michigan State's J Batt as athletics director
cards.teaser: The University of Kentucky named J Batt as its new athletics director and CEO of Champions Blue.
cards.body:
Kentucky has appointed J Batt as its new athletics director and CEO of Champions Blue. Batt previously held a position at Michigan State, bringing leadership experience to the Wildcats' program.

The move has created disruption at Michigan State. Basketball coach Tom Izzo expressed frustration with Batt's departure, calling it "kind of disgusting," and indicated he is working to address the resulting leadership gap. Former Michigan State athletics director Mark Hollis has expressed willingness to return to the role if the opportunity arises.

cards.headline: Bukayo Saka says he will continue managing fitness risks for England
cards.teaser: The England winger said he is ready to play in Wednesday's World Cup opener against Croatia.
cards.body:
Bukayo Saka has admitted he is continuing to gamble on his fitness to play for England at the World Cup, but insists he is "ready to go" for Wednesday's opener against Croatia. The Arsenal forward has been managing a nagging achilles injury that he picked up during the Carabao Cup final in March.

Manager Thomas Tuchel is carefully monitoring Saka's condition. The 24-year-old came off the bench in England's final warm-up match against Costa Rica and has completed 90 minutes only once in his last five appearances for Arsenal.

cards.headline: VAR official attributes hand gesture to involuntary twitch
cards.teaser: Video assistant referee Shaun Evans denied making an intentional hand gesture during a match.
cards.body:
Video assistant referee Shaun Evans has denied intentionally making a hand gesture to communicate any message, affiliation, game or belief. Evans characterized the gesture as an involuntary and subconscious twitch, claiming he was unaware he had made it at the time.

The incident drew scrutiny from observers during a World Cup broadcast. Evans' explanation attributes the movement to an unintentional physical response rather than a purposeful signal.

cards.headline: Hydration breaks at World Cup draw debate over tactical impact
cards.teaser: BBC pundits discussed how official hydration breaks are affecting matches at the 2026 World Cup.
cards.body:
BBC Sport pundits Micah Richards, Theo Walcott, and Olivier Giroud have debated the impact of hydration breaks at the 2026 World Cup. The scheduled stoppages, introduced to protect player welfare during matches played in warm conditions, have sparked discussion about their effect on gameplay.

The breaks are reshaping how teams approach tactics and momentum during matches, according to the pundits' discussion. The pauses give teams opportunities to regroup and adjust their strategies mid-game, fundamentally altering the flow and tactical dynamics of World Cup fixtures.

cards.headline: Scotland manager Steve Clarke doing cartwheels reflects team culture shift
cards.teaser: Reporter Amy Canavan described changes in atmosphere around the Scotland squad in Charlotte.
cards.body:
Steve Clarke has been doing cartwheels at breakfast during Scotland's World Cup campaign in Charlotte, signaling a notable shift in team culture. According to reporting from the camp, the manager's playful behavior reflects a broader change in atmosphere among the squad and staff.

The relaxed energy extends beyond breakfast, with players and staff enjoying more informal moments together, including time kicking a ball about in Boston. This represents a departure from the mood in previous tournaments, demonstrating how Clarke has reshaped the environment within the Scotland camp.

hero.headline: Ian McKellen Says He Invoked Trump's Mar-a-Lago While Filming Avengers: Doomsday
hero.body:
At a Rome film festival, Sir Ian McKellen shared how he tapped into real-world frustration while filming an upcoming Marvel superhero movie. The 87-year-old actor, who returns as the X-Men villain Magneto in Avengers: Doomsday, revealed an unconventional method for summoning intense emotion during an action sequence.

McKellen told the crowd of 2,000 at an open-air cinema that he was shooting a scene where his character destroys a New Jersey location. When directors Anthony and Joe Russo asked him to appear more furious, McKellen found an effective solution. "I stood there and I shouted: 'Mar-a-Lago!'" he explained, referring to Donald Trump's Florida resort and private club.

The anecdote demonstrates McKellen's creative approach to performance and his willingness to draw on contemporary political feelings to enhance his acting. The actor rose from his seat during the Rome appearance to physically reenact the moment for the audience.

Avengers: Doomsday marks a significant return for McKellen to the Marvel Cinematic Universe. The film also brings back Sir Patrick Stewart, reuniting the original X-Men cast with the MCU's main storyline. Directed by the Russo Brothers, who previously helmed Avengers: Endgame, the film is scheduled for December release. It will serve as the MCU's 39th feature and functions as a sequel to Endgame, which earned 2.8 billion dollars and remains the second highest-grossing film ever made.

Beyond his Avengers work, McKellen is experiencing a career resurgence following a stage fall in 2024. He earned critical acclaim for his performance in Steven Soderbergh's The Christophers and participated in an innovative video stage installation in New York this year. McKellen has also remained active in social causes, recently joining a march against the criminalization of LGBTQ+ people in Commonwealth countries and unveiling an English Heritage blue plaque honoring Laurence Olivier's former London home.

The actor is also preparing to return to another iconic role. He revealed plans to travel to New Zealand to reprise Gandalf in The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum. Directed by Andy Serkis, who also returns as the character Gollum, the film will tell a story McKellen noted was not written by J.R.R. Tolkien himself. Producer Peter Jackson is overseeing the project.

McKellen's appearance at the Cinema in Piazza festival, a free series organized by the Piccolo America Foundation, allowed him to share both the Avengers footage and personal reflections on his career. The festival features open-air screenings and Q&A sessions with filmmakers and actors.

cards.headline: Smashing Pumpkins and Chris Stapleton to Headline Fourth of July Benefit Concert
cards.teaser: The rock band and country star will perform at a Los Angeles event supporting Feeding America.
cards.body:
The Smashing Pumpkins and Chris Stapleton will headline Americas Block Party, a benefit concert scheduled for Fourth of July in Los Angeles. Proceeds from ticket sales after fees will go to Feeding America, a nationwide network of food banks and food rescue organizations.

The event brings together artists from different musical genres for a charitable cause. Feeding America works to address hunger across the United States through its network of partner organizations. The concert represents a collaboration between major music acts and philanthropic efforts around a national holiday.

cards.headline: New York Knicks to Appear on The Tonight Show Following NBA Finals Win
cards.teaser: The team will join Wu-Tang Clan on the late-night program after their championship victory.
cards.body:
The New York Knicks will appear on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon after winning the NBA Finals, defeating the Spurs to clinch the title. The team will share the stage with hip-hop group Wu-Tang Clan for the late-night appearance.

Since The Tonight Show tapes in New York City, it provided an ideal platform for the local franchise to celebrate their historic championship. Viewers can watch the episode for free through standard broadcast television.

cards.headline: RisingJoy Launches Microdrama Streaming Service on TikTok
cards.teaser: The Singapore-based company debuts RJOY with 20 original titles available in the U.S. and Japan.
cards.body:
RisingJoy has launched RJOY, a microdrama streaming service initially available to audiences in the United States and Japan through TikTok Minis. The service features 20 original titles at launch. TikTok Minis is an in-app feature that provides access to vertical content.

Cassandra Yang, CEO and co-founder of the Singapore-based company, announced the launch at the APOS conference in Bali. The direct-to-consumer service represents an expansion into streaming for RisingJoy. Microdramas are short-form serialized content designed for mobile viewing, a format that has gained popularity in Asian markets.

cards.headline: The Linda Lindas Sign With Reprise-Warner Records
cards.teaser: The Los Angeles quartet released a new single and video to mark the deal.
cards.body:
Los Angeles quartet The Linda Lindas has signed with Reprise-Warner Records. The group, which first gained national attention in 2018 when its members were teenagers or pre-teenagers, celebrated the signing by releasing a new single and video titled "Burning Out."

The band described the song as feeling simultaneously new and nostalgic. The release is likely a precursor to a third album from the group. The Linda Lindas have built their following through energetic performances and punk-influenced music that resonates with younger audiences.

cards.headline: West Wilson Exits Summer House After Three Seasons
cards.teaser: The reality star's contract was not renewed for the show's 11th season, which begins filming in July.
cards.body:
West Wilson will not be returning for Season 11 of Bravo's Summer House. His contract was not renewed, according to sources. Filming for the upcoming season is set to begin in the Hamptons in early July.

Wilson was a cast member for three seasons on the reality series, which follows a group of friends sharing a summer house in the Hamptons. His departure comes after the show delivered its most-watched season to date, driven by a significant cast scandal that generated sustained media attention.

cards.headline: amfAR to Honor Artist Marina Abramović at Venice Gala
cards.teaser: The performance artist will be recognized at the sixth annual amfAR Venezia benefit in September.
cards.body:
The amfAR Venezia benefit gala will honor conceptual and performance artist Marina Abramović at its sixth annual event on September 6 in Venice, Italy. amfAR CEO Kyle Clifford said the organization is recognizing the humanitarian impact of Abramović's work and philanthropy.

Clifford described Abramović's groundbreaking artistry and dedication to people living with HIV and AIDS as inspirational. The annual Venice gala is part of amfAR's ongoing fundraising and awareness efforts for HIV and AIDS research and treatment. Abramović is known for her pioneering work in performance art spanning several decades.

hero.headline: CIA director questions Iran's commitment to nuclear concessions
hero.teaser: CIA Director John Ratcliffe told senior officials that US intelligence raises doubts about Iran's willingness to make nuclear concessions.
hero.body:
CIA Director John Ratcliffe has told President Trump and other senior officials that intelligence gathered by US agencies has raised serious doubts about Iran's willingness to make the nuclear concessions the US is seeking in any final deal, according to sources familiar with those discussions.

Ratcliffe is not alone in his skepticism within Trump's top team. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth have both expressed concerns and raised questions about the deal in internal discussions, according to two sources. The divided views among senior officials reflect broader uncertainty about Iran's intentions as the two countries prepare for 60 days of nuclear negotiations.

The skepticism comes as the administration moves forward with a memorandum of understanding signed digitally over the weekend. Senior US officials told reporters that the MOU is only the initial step toward a broader agreement. The agreement between the US and Iran is intended to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and kick-start the 60-day negotiation period, with the deal set to be signed in person on Friday.

In contrast to the concerns raised by Ratcliffe, Rubio, and Hegseth, Vice President Vance and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have advocated for the deal, according to sources familiar with the discussions.

The skepticism about Iran's nuclear intentions carries significant weight given recent diplomatic history. Previous nuclear negotiations have been complicated by misunderstandings about Iran's nuclear program, including disagreements over technical aspects and the scope of Iran's planned nuclear activities.

The ongoing negotiations represent an attempt to resolve a conflict that began on February 28 and disrupted energy production and transportation across the Middle East. Oil prices jumped when the fighting began, and the new agreement aims to stabilize global energy markets by reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

This is not the first time US officials have had to navigate nuclear discussions with Iran. The Obama administration previously conducted extensive nuclear negotiations, sending 10 senior officials from four different departments to talks in Vienna in 2009. Those negotiations stretched over three 24-hour days, with negotiators in constant touch with Washington to check details of the proposed deal.

The Trump administration's current negotiating team appears leaner. Sources indicate that the talks leading up to the current MOU involved limited technical expertise and support compared to previous diplomatic efforts.

The next 60 days will be crucial for determining whether the two countries can reach a comprehensive nuclear agreement. The internal divisions among US officials suggest that reaching consensus on Iran's nuclear program will require navigating significant disagreements about Iran's reliability as a negotiating partner and the likelihood of achieving US objectives.

cards.headline: US and Iran reach agreement to reopen Strait of Hormuz and begin nuclear talks
cards.teaser: The United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding over the weekend to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and begin 60 days of nuclear negotiations, senio.
cards.body:
The United States and Iran have announced a framework peace deal ending their 15-week conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global shipping route. Iran's Supreme National Security Council confirmed that military operations on all fronts, including Lebanon, will cease permanently starting Monday night.

The agreement addresses the immediate conflict but leaves critical issues for further negotiations, particularly regarding Iran's nuclear program. The deal has sparked optimism in financial markets and offers potential relief for the Middle East and global economy, though the precise terms remain subject to ongoing discussions between the two countries.

cards.headline: Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche begins Senate confirmation meetings
cards.teaser: Todd Blanche met with Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Chuck Grassley as he launches a monthlong confirmation process.
cards.body:
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche began meeting with Republican senators as he launches a monthlong confirmation process. Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, was Blanche's first stop. The committee will process his nomination before it moves to the full Senate.

Grassley issued a positive statement about Blanche's career following their meeting. The Iowa senator said he appreciated the opportunity to meet with the acting attorney general. Blanche will continue meeting with senators in the coming weeks as part of the standard confirmation process for cabinet-level positions.

cards.headline: House Democrat warns of subpoenas for Trump officials if party wins majority
cards.teaser: Rep. Robert Garcia said acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and other Trump officials would likely face subpoenas immediately after Democrats take control.
cards.body:
Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, said acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and other Trump administration officials are likely to face subpoenas on day one of a Democratic majority if the party takes control of the lower chamber after the midterm elections.

Garcia outlined plans for aggressive oversight of the Trump administration should Democrats win the House. The California Democrat's comments reflect the party's strategy to use congressional investigative powers to scrutinize executive branch actions. Garcia serves as the ranking member on the oversight committee, positioning him to lead such investigations if Democrats gain the majority.

cards.headline: Republicans fund Democratic primary candidates viewed as easier to defeat
cards.teaser: House Democrats are criticizing what appears to be a nationwide Republican effort to elevate Democratic primary candidates seen as more beatable in November.
cards.body:
House Democrats are criticizing what appears to be a nationwide Republican effort to elevate Democratic primary candidates viewed as more beatable in November. The practice, once rare, is becoming commonplace. Democrats used similar tactics in 2022 and 2024, with one House Democrat describing it as the new normal.

Republican former Rep. Adam Kinzinger called GOP spending in Democratic primaries awful but said it was inevitable after Democrats adopted the tactic during the Biden years. The cross-party interference in primaries represents a shift in campaign strategy, with both parties now willing to invest resources in opposition primaries to influence general election matchups.

cards.headline: Green algae reappear at Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool after renovation
cards.teaser: Images show green algae have returned to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool despite President Trump's recent renovation.
cards.body:
Images of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool show that green algae have returned to the site on the National Mall despite President Trump's renovations. The project cost more than $13 million and included the addition of nanobubbler technology that has successfully destroyed the algae, according to the Interior Department.

An Interior Department spokesperson addressed the algae's reappearance. The renovation was intended to permanently address the recurring algae problem that has plagued the reflecting pool for years. The nanobubbler technology was installed as part of the broader effort to maintain water quality at the iconic memorial site.

cards.headline: Former ICE director takes consulting role in national security and defense
cards.teaser: Todd Lyons, former ICE leader, has taken a new job consulting on national security and defense matters.
cards.body:
Todd Lyons, former director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, has taken on a consulting role focused on national security and defense. The transition marks his move from federal law enforcement to the private sector.

Federal law prevents Lyons from engaging with the Department of Homeland Security for one year following his departure. This cooling-off period is a standard restriction for senior government officials who move to private sector positions involving their former areas of responsibility.
